docs.title: Continuous facial recognition, built into your app
docs.text:
The YEO CFR SDK lets your app enrol a user's face and confirm that the right person is present, at sign-in and throughout the session. It runs on the phone. These pages show you how to build it, what we recommend, and what your security and compliance teams will want to know.

docs.title: The short version
docs.text:
• Continuous. The SDK reports on every analysed camera frame, so your app can check who is present at any point in a session, not only at login.
  • On the device. Enrolment, recognition and liveness run on the phone. The SDK does not send faces, face samples or results anywhere.
  • No photos kept. The SDK saves numeric face samples, not images.
  • Your app holds the data. Encryption, backup rules and deletion of the saved enrolment are your app's decisions. We explain how.
  • Nothing for the user to perform. The liveness check is passive. The user just looks at the camera.
  • A credential is required. The SDK needs a credential from YEO. Contact YEO to get one.

Which versions these pages describe

Android 0.2.29, iOS 0.11.2, React Native 0.5.2, Flutter 0.5.1, Capacitor 0.5.0 and Cordova 0.5.0. See Published versions.

docs.title: Data and privacy
docs.text: Written for your security, privacy and compliance teams. It describes the published versions listed on Published versions.

docs.title: In short
docs.text:
• Face processing happens on the phone. The SDK makes no network connection of its own.
  • The SDK saves numeric face samples, never photos or video.
  • Your app controls the saved enrolment, including where it is kept and how it is encrypted. The SDK does not encrypt it by default.
  • On Android, Google components used for face detection have their own network activity. See below.
  • Device trust and proof of a result to your backend are your app's responsibility. See below.

docs.title: What the SDK stores
docs.text:
Stored Details Enrolled names Whatever your app passes as the name. We recommend an opaque ID. Face samples Up to 25 from enrolment and up to 25 recent ones per person. Each is a set of numbers computed from one camera frame. Timestamps and version details When the person was enrolled, the format version, and the recognition model's version.

The SDK does not store photos, video or camera frames. Frames are processed in memory and are not saved.

keepFaceImagesInTracker on Android

The Android API reference lists this option and describes storing images. That wording comes from an earlier engine. In Android 0.2.29 the option has no effect, and no image is stored with either value.

For where the enrolment goes by default on each platform, see Store the gallery.

docs.title: From the SDK
docs.text:
Nothing. The SDK sends no faces, samples, names, results or usage data to YEO or anyone else. It contains no analytics or crash-reporting product, and the SDK itself declares no internet permission. Starting the SDK with your credential does not contact YEO either.

Your app can of course send data itself. For example, it may upload an encrypted gallery if you choose to keep one on your server.

docs.title: On iOS
docs.text: Nothing beyond the SDK statement above. Face detection uses Apple's Vision framework, which is part of iOS and runs on the device. The SDK uses no Google code on iOS.

docs.title: On Android
docs.text:
Face detection uses Google's ML Kit, through Google Play services. This is separate from the SDK:

  • Model download. The face detection model is not inside your app. Google Play services downloads and updates it, starting on first use.
  • Usage metrics. ML Kit sends Google its own diagnostics and usage metrics, such as device and app information, performance and error codes. Google states that images and detection results stay on the device. The SDK does not turn this logging off.
  • Permissions. ML Kit adds INTERNET and ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE to your app's merged manifest.

Google's terms make the app developer responsible for telling users about this and for the Google Play Data safety form. Read Google's ML Kit data disclosure and the ML Kit terms.

docs.title: At build time
docs.text: These happen on your build machines, not on users' phones: the iOS Swift package comes from GitHub, and the Android package comes from YEO's private Maven repository.

docs.title: Models
docs.text: YEO's recognition and liveness models are bundled inside the SDK. They change only when you ship an SDK update in your own app, and the SDK does not download them.

docs.title: Encryption and who is responsible
docs.text:
Topic The SDK Your app Processing of faces Happens on the phone Encryption of the saved enrolment Not encrypted by default. iOS offers a hook for your own cipher. Encrypts it, with keys in the Keychain or Keystore Location of the saved enrolment Private storage, where a built-in store is used Chooses it, or takes over storage Backup and device transfer Excluded by Capacitor and Cordova only Excludes it everywhere else Deletion Provides the calls Calls them, and removes its own copies Network transfer Does none Protects anything it sends Privacy notices and consent Yours to provide Retention Keeps samples until cleared Sets the policy

See Store the gallery for how to do each of these.

docs.title: Device and app security
docs.text:
The SDK's liveness check looks at what is shown to the camera. The SDK does not assess the device or app it runs on, so these are for your app to handle.

Threat In the SDK? What we suggest Rooted or jailbroken device Not detected Google Play Integrity or Apple App Attest in your app, and your own policy to block or step up Emulator Not detected The same device checks Hooking or tampering tools Not detected Runtime protection or app shielding, if your policy requires it Screen sharing or capture Not detected or blocked FLAG_SECURE on the Android face screen, and screen-capture checks on iOS Virtual camera No check on where frames come from Rely on the device checks above. On Android, make sure your app opens the device's front camera.

docs.title: Results are not signed
docs.text:
The SDK returns results to your app as ordinary data structures. It does not sign them, and it does not use a hardware-backed key to do so. To rely on a result on your server, use your own protections, such as App Attest or Play Integrity and your existing secure channel.

Think of the result as local

A result proves something to your app on that device. Design your backend so that a decision is bound to your own session and device checks.

docs.title: Biometric data
docs.text: The gallery is biometric data. Check your obligations under the rules that apply to you, and treat it accordingly in your records, notices and retention policy. These pages describe what the software does. They are not legal advice.

docs.title: Questions from your compliance team
docs.text: Common questions are answered in the FAQ. For anything else, contact YEO.

docs.title: What does "continuous" mean?
docs.text: The SDK reports on every analysed camera frame, so your app can confirm that the right person is present throughout a period you choose, not only at login. See Verify throughout a session.

docs.title: Do users get prompted during a session?
docs.text: The SDK does not prompt anyone. The check is passive, and your app decides whether and when to show a message.

docs.title: What happens if the check fails during a session?
docs.text: Your app decides. It might ask the user to verify again, hide sensitive content, block a risky action, flag the session or end it. The SDK provides the signal, and your app controls the response.

docs.title: Does it replace our login or identity checks?
docs.text: No. It runs alongside your existing login and onboarding, without changes to that infrastructure.

docs.title: Do we need servers to run it?
docs.text: No. Processing happens on each phone, so there is no YEO server for you to run or call.

docs.title: Does it work in a web browser?
docs.text: No. The SDK runs in iOS and Android apps. Web apps can use it through a Capacitor or Cordova shell, but not in a browser on its own.

docs.title: Can it match our brand?
docs.text: Yes. The SDK has no YEO-branded screens in your app. Your app owns the layout, wording and prompts.

docs.title: How long does enrolment take?
docs.text: It depends on your app's capture screen. A quick capture takes about a second. The guided capture we recommend for production, with a few small head turns, takes from about 5 seconds to around a minute.

docs.title: How many photos are stored?
docs.text: None. The SDK stores numeric face samples, not images: up to 25 from enrolment and up to 25 recent ones per person.

docs.title: Does it work with glasses?
docs.text: Yes, with clear everyday glasses. If the user sometimes wears glasses and sometimes does not, capture part of the enrolment each way. Sunglasses should be removed.

docs.title: Does it work with a face mask, hat or hood?
docs.text: Please remove them for enrolment and sign-in. Covering the nose and mouth, or shadowing the eyes, prevents reliable recognition.

docs.title: What about beards, haircuts, make-up and ageing?
docs.text: Gradual changes may be absorbed, because successful sign-ins can refresh a set of recent samples where your app saves them. See Getting better over time. After a large sudden change, such as shaving a full beard, re-enrol if recognition becomes unreliable.

docs.title: Can several people be enrolled in one app?
docs.text: We recommend one person per app installation. If you need several, contact YEO first so that we can advise on identity handling for your platform.

docs.title: What does the user see if enrolment fails?
docs.text: Your app decides the wording. The SDK reports when no face, several faces or a badly placed face is in view. A good capture screen shows the framing hint and a progress indicator, and shows tips after about a minute without progress.

docs.title: Does the enrolment capture check liveness?
docs.text: It depends on the platform. On Android, the React Native, Capacitor and Cordova captures only count live frames, and native Android and Flutter samples check liveness before enrolling. On iPhone, the camera capture stores a frame with one face and does not check liveness itself. See Protect the enrolment step.

docs.title: What is the recognition threshold?
docs.text: A similarity of 0.35 on the SDK's 0 to 1 scale is the default bar for a match. YEO set it from internal testing, and your app does not need to choose one. Please talk to YEO before you consider changing anything related to it.

docs.title: What are the false accept and false reject rates?
docs.text: They depend heavily on your users, devices and lighting, so we do not quote a single figure. YEO can discuss an evaluation on your target devices and conditions.

docs.title: Can identical twins unlock each other's account?
docs.text: Face recognition, ours included, cannot reliably tell identical twins apart. For sensitive actions, use face sign-in together with your other security checks.

docs.title: What distance should the user hold the phone at?
docs.text: About 30 to 40 cm, with the whole face in the picture. The framing hint says "move closer" or "move back" when needed.

docs.title: Does it need an internet connection?
docs.text: Recognition and liveness run on the phone. On iOS no connection is needed. On Android, Google Play services must be present, and it needs a connection to download the face detection model the first time.

docs.title: Does the user have to blink, smile or turn their head?
docs.text: No. Liveness is passive: the user just looks at the camera. Any head-turn prompts during enrolment are there to capture varied samples for recognition, not to test liveness.

docs.title: Why does it say "not live" for a moment at first?
docs.text: The check judges a short sequence of frames, so it needs about a second, occasionally a few seconds, before its first answer. Show "Checking…" during that time rather than an error.

docs.title: Why does liveness flicker near a window?
docs.text: Strong light behind the user underexposes the face and makes both recognition and liveness less certain. Ask the user to turn and face the light.

docs.title: Two people are in view. What happens?
docs.text: Liveness is decided for one face, so the frame is not accepted until only one face remains. Show "One face at a time".

docs.title: Which value should our app use to decide liveness?
docs.text: isLive or status in the plugins, update.status on iOS, and faceState == Detected && isConfident() in native Android. Do not compare confidence with a number: it is for display, and its scale can change between SDK versions.

docs.title: Can a photo or a video of the user fool it?
docs.text: The check is designed to refuse common attacks, such as printed photos and photos or videos shown on a screen, and your app should accept recognition only together with liveness. Like any liveness system, it lowers the risk but cannot rule out every attack. Use it with your other security measures for high-value actions.

docs.title: Can we feed our own camera frames or stored photos?
docs.text: Yes, the plugins and native SDKs accept frames from your own pipeline. Liveness only means something on a live camera stream, because frames replayed from storage cannot prove the person is present. Still-image matching runs recognition only.

docs.title: Where is the enrolment stored, and is it encrypted?
docs.text: On the device, in a place your app controls. The SDK does not encrypt it by default. For production, we recommend that your app encrypts it with a key in the iOS Keychain or Android Keystore and excludes it from cloud backup. See Store the gallery.

docs.title: Does any data leave the phone?
docs.text: The SDK sends nothing. On Android, Google's ML Kit, which the SDK uses for face detection, sends Google its own usage metrics and downloads its model through Google Play services. Google states that images and detection results stay on the device. See What leaves the device.

docs.title: Can we back up enrolments to the cloud or move them to a new phone?
docs.text: We recommend keeping enrolments on the device and excluding them from cloud backup, because they are biometric data. On a new phone, the user should enrol again.

docs.title: Can we store galleries on our server?
docs.text: The gallery is available as data you can store, but it is biometric data and must be protected in transit and at rest. Record which SDK version made each one, because a gallery from an older recognition model cannot be loaded by a newer one.

docs.title: How do we delete a user's face data?
docs.text: Use the clear call for your platform and delete any copies you hold. See How to delete it.

docs.title: How big is the saved enrolment?
docs.text: About 4 KB for one sample, about 90 KB for a person with all 25 enrolment samples, and about 185 KB with both sets full.

docs.title: Will users have to re-enrol after an app update?
docs.text: Not for an update within the current versions. Moving from an older version with a different recognition model needs a one-time re-enrolment. See Upgrade and re-enrol.

docs.title: What happens to an old enrolment after the upgrade?
docs.text: The SDK refuses it safely. Your app sees that nobody is enrolled and should ask the user to enrol again. Delete the old file once the user has re-enrolled.

docs.title: Do we need a licence?
docs.text: Yes. The SDK needs a credential from YEO. Contact YEO.

docs.title: What happens if the credential is refused?
docs.text: The SDK does not run. On Android you get an error your app can handle. On iOS the app closes during start-up. See Before you start.

docs.title: Does activating the SDK send anything to YEO?
docs.text: No. The SDK makes no network connection of its own, including during activation.

docs.title: Does it work in a simulator or emulator?
docs.text: Your app builds and runs there, but recognition needs a real phone and a real face.

docs.title: Does it work on Android phones without Google Play services?
docs.text: No. These versions need Google Play services for face detection.

docs.title: Which operating systems are supported?
docs.text: Android 7.0 (API 24) or later, and iOS 17.0 or later. See Before you start.

docs.title: Does the SDK detect rooted or jailbroken phones?
docs.text: No. The SDK does not check for rooted or jailbroken devices, emulators, hooking tools, screen capture or virtual cameras. Your app handles these, for example with Google Play Integrity or Apple App Attest. See Device and app security.

docs.title: Are results signed?
docs.text: No. Results are returned to your app as ordinary data structures. To rely on a result on your server, use your own attestation and secure channel.

docs.title: Does the SDK contain analytics or crash reporting?
docs.text: No. On Android, ML Kit has its own usage metrics, as described in What leaves the device.

docs.title: Are models updated over the air?
docs.text: YEO's recognition and liveness models are not. They are bundled in the SDK and change when you ship an SDK update. On Android, Google Play services delivers and updates the separate face detection model.

docs.title: Does the SDK store face images on the device?
docs.text: No, on either platform. The Android option keepFaceImagesInTracker has no effect in these versions.

docs.title: Can we wrap our app with a shielding or hardening product?
docs.text: Yes. Those products change the app the camera runs in, so run your acceptance tests on a shielded build. See the Go-live checklist.

docs.text:
Pick the page for the technology your app is built with. Each one takes you from an empty integration to a first enrolment and a first recognition.

Your app is built with Start here Full integration guide Kotlin or Java Android API reference Swift iOS API reference React Native React Native React Native guide Flutter Flutter Plugin README (access from YEO) Capacitor Capacitor Capacitor guide Cordova Cordova Cordova guide

Not sure between Capacitor and Cordova? If your project has a config.xml and a platforms/ folder at its root, it is a Cordova app. If it has capacitor.config.ts or capacitor.config.json, it is a Capacitor app.

Read Before you start first. It lists what to ask YEO for and what every platform needs.

docs.title: Get started on Android
docs.text: Version 0.2.29. You provide the camera frames, and the SDK gives you a result for each one.

docs.title: 1. Add the SDK
docs.text:
YEO support gives you the repository address and a login. Keep them outside source control, for example in ~/.gradle/gradle.properties.

repositories {
    maven {
        url = uri(providers.gradleProperty("yeoMavenUrl").get())
        credentials {
            username = providers.gradleProperty("yeoMavenUser").get()
            password = providers.gradleProperty("yeoMavenPassword").get()
        }
    }
}
dependencies {
    implementation("com.yeomessaging:yeofr-android:0.2.29")
}

Your app needs minSdk 24, compileSdk 36 and Android Gradle Plugin 8.9.1 or later.

docs.title: 2. Start the SDK
docs.text:
YEOFRSDK.init(context, code = credentialFromYeo)

init throws an exception if YEO's credential is missing or refused. See Before you start.

docs.title: 3. Send camera frames
docs.text:
Build one ImageFrameParameters per frame and call detectFaces from a single thread. The fastest hand-off is raw ARGB32 from an upright bitmap.

val buffer = ByteBuffer.allocate(bitmap.rowBytes * bitmap.height)
bitmap.copyPixelsToBuffer(buffer)
val params = ImageFrameParameters(
    height = bitmap.height,
    width = bitmap.width,
    scanline = bitmap.rowBytes,
    ratio = 1.0,
    buffer = buffer.array(),
    bufferSize = buffer.capacity(),
    uuid = UUID.randomUUID(),
)
val result = YEOFRSDK.detectFaces(params)

docs.title: 4. Enrol the user
docs.text:
Enrol only from a frame with one live face. Each enroll call adds one sample, so call it several times across a short capture. See Enrol a user.

if (result.faceState == FaceRecognitionState.Detected && result.isConfident()) {
    val faceId = result.faceIDs.keys.first()
    YEOFRSDK.enroll(faceId, "user-id", learnFromCurrentFrame = true)   // 0 means success
}

docs.title: 5. Save the gallery
docs.text:
The SDK hands the enrolment to your app as bytes, and it never writes them to disk itself. Your app decides where they go and encrypts them. See Store the gallery.

val gallery: ByteArray? = YEOFRSDK.faceRecognitionTrackerData()   // save this
val code = YEOFRSDK.loadTracker(gallery)                          // negative means refused

docs.title: 6. Recognise the user
docs.text:
val live = result.faceState == FaceRecognitionState.Detected && result.isConfident()
val recognised = live && result.faceIDs.values.any { it.isNotEmpty() }

Accept only once this has held for about a second. See Recognise a user.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: Three things save the most time: get your access from YEO early, test on real phones, and decide where the saved enrolment will live.

docs.title: Get your credential
docs.text:
The SDK needs a credential from YEO, and it will not run without one. Contact YEO support to get one.

Handle it like this:

  • Keep it out of your source code. Load it from your build configuration or your backend, so that a new credential does not need a new app release.
  • Cover your whole test period. Credentials have an expiry date. Ask YEO for the next one before the current one runs out.
  • Check it before every release, on both platforms. A refused credential does not behave the same everywhere:
Platform What happens when the credential is refused Android YEOFRSDK.init throws an exception. iOS The app closes during start-up. You cannot catch this, and it looks like a crash. React Native, Capacitor, Cordova On Android the call rejects with an error. On iOS the app closes, as above. Flutter On Android YeoFR.init throws a PlatformException with code INIT_ERROR. On iOS the app closes, as above.

If your iOS app closes when the face screen opens

Check the credential first.

docs.title: Get access to the Android package
docs.text:
The Android SDK is in a private Maven repository. YEO support gives you its address and a login. You need these for Android builds on every platform, including React Native, Flutter, Capacitor and Cordova.

Keep the address and login out of source control. Put them in ~/.gradle/gradle.properties on developer machines and in secret environment variables on your build server.

The iOS SDK is distributed from a public Swift package, so it needs no login.

docs.title: What every platform needs
docs.text:
Android iOS Operating system Android 7.0 (API 24) or later iOS 17.0 or later Device A real phone with Google Play services A real iPhone. A TrueDepth camera is recommended. Build tools compileSdk 36 and Android Gradle Plugin 8.9.1 or later Swift 5.9 or later. Bridge plugins have their own Xcode requirement: see their pages. Permission Camera Camera (NSCameraUsageDescription)

Test on real phones

Recognition needs a real device and a real face. Apps build and run in the simulator or emulator, but you will not get a real recognition result there. This is expected.

Google Play services on Android

Face detection on Android is delivered through Google Play services, and the face model downloads on first use. Phones without Google Play services are not supported, and the first use needs a network connection.

docs.title: Decide three things early
docs.text:
1. Where the saved enrolment lives. On the phone, encrypted by your app, is what we recommend. See Store the gallery.
  2. How the user gets back in without their face. Face sign-in needs a fallback such as a PIN or a password, for failed attempts and for moments when the user must enrol again.
  3. One person per app installation. This is the setup we recommend. If you need several people on one installation, talk to YEO first, because identity handling differs by platform.

docs.title: Get started with Capacitor
docs.text: Version 0.5.0, which uses the Android SDK 0.2.29 and the iOS SDK 0.11.2. It works with any web framework in a Capacitor 7 or 8 shell, with or without Ionic. The native layer owns the camera and draws the preview behind your page. Your page gets small JSON events, and camera frames never reach JavaScript.

docs.title: Web frameworks
docs.text:
The plugin works with Angular, React, Vue, Svelte and plain JavaScript, with or without Ionic. The calls on this page are the same in all of them.

The Capacitor guide has an Ionic Angular quick start. In other frameworks, start the camera when the face page opens and stop it when the page closes.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
npm install @yeomessagingcom/capacitor-yeofr
npx cap sync

iOS:

  • Set the deployment target of the App target to 17.0, then run npx cap sync again.
  • Add NSCameraUsageDescription to Info.plist.
  • You need Xcode 26 or later.
  • On Capacitor 8, use Swift Package Manager. On Capacitor 7, use CocoaPods and add the YEOFR Swift package to the App target at exact version 0.11.2.

Android:

  • Add the address and login from YEO to ~/.gradle/gradle.properties, or to environment variables on your build server.
  • Add the plugin's repository and core module settings, as shown in the Capacitor guide.
  • Build with compileSdk 36 and Android Gradle Plugin 8.9.1 or later.

Your page: make it transparent where the camera should show. The guide shows how. Lock the page or app to portrait, because the preview does not follow device rotation.

docs.title: 2. Activate and listen
docs.text:
import { Yeofr } from '@yeomessagingcom/capacitor-yeofr';

await Yeofr.activate({ pilotCode: credentialFromYeo });   // once per process
const results = await Yeofr.addListener('result', (r) => {
  // r.status: 'noFace' | 'badFraming' | 'notTrusted' | 'trusted'
  // r.matchedName, r.isLive, r.framing
});
await Yeofr.start();

On Android a refused credential rejects with activationFailed. On iOS it closes the app. See Before you start.

docs.title: 3. Enrol the user
docs.text:
await Yeofr.enrol({
  name: customerId,
  poses: ['front', 'yawLeft', 'yawRight', 'pitchUp', 'pitchDown'],
});
// 'enrolProgress' events arrive, then 'registered'

The plugin keeps one identity at a time. A new capture replaces the old one, and a capture that is cut short puts the previous enrolment back. See Enrol a user.

docs.title: 4. Recognise the user
docs.text:
Act only on status === 'trusted', and check that matchedName is the person you expect. See Recognise a user.

await Yeofr.stop();
await results.remove();

docs.title: 5. Decide where the template is kept
docs.text: By default the plugin keeps it in private app storage, out of device backups, and does not encrypt it. We recommend storing it encrypted: read it with getTrackerData() and put it back with loadTracker(). See Store the gallery.

docs.title: Get started with Cordova
docs.text: Version 0.5.0, which uses the Android SDK 0.2.29 and the iOS SDK 0.11.2. It works with any web framework on Cordova, including Ionic Angular apps. The calls, events and statuses are the same as in the Capacitor plugin.

docs.title: Web frameworks
docs.text:
The plugin works with Angular, React, Vue, Svelte and plain JavaScript, with or without Ionic. The calls on this page are the same in all of them.

The Cordova guide has an Ionic Angular quick start. In other frameworks, start the camera when the face page opens and stop it when the page closes.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
cordova plugin add @yeomessagingcom/cordova-plugin-yeofr

Android (cordova-android 14 recommended, 13 supported with one more setting):

  • Add the address and login from YEO to ~/.gradle/gradle.properties, or to environment variables on your build server.
  • Build with JDK 17 or later.
  • Add these to config.xml:
<platform name="android">
    <preference name="android-minSdkVersion" value="24" />
    <preference name="android-compileSdkVersion" value="36" />
    <preference name="AndroidGradlePluginVersion" value="8.9.1" />
    <preference name="AndroidJavaSourceCompatibility" value="17" />
    <preference name="AndroidJavaTargetCompatibility" value="17" />
</platform>

iOS (cordova-ios 8 recommended, 7 supported):

  • Set deployment-target to 17.0 in config.xml.
  • The plugin adds a default camera usage text. You can reword it when you add the plugin, as the guide shows.
  • You need Xcode 26 or later.

Your page: make it transparent where the camera should show, and lock the app to portrait.

The Cordova guide walks through all of this, with a full Ionic Angular example.

docs.title: 2. Activate and listen
docs.text:
The plugin is available as cordova.plugins.Yeofr after deviceready.

const Yeofr = cordova.plugins.Yeofr;

await Yeofr.activate({ pilotCode: credentialFromYeo });
const results = await Yeofr.addListener('result', (r) => {
  // r.status: 'noFace' | 'badFraming' | 'notTrusted' | 'trusted'
});
await Yeofr.start();

On Android a refused credential rejects with activationFailed. On iOS it closes the app. See Before you start.

docs.title: 3. Enrol the user
docs.text:
await Yeofr.enrol({
  name: customerId,
  poses: ['front', 'yawLeft', 'yawRight', 'pitchUp', 'pitchDown'],
});
// 'enrolProgress' events arrive, then 'registered'

See Enrol a user.

docs.title: 4. Recognise the user
docs.text: Act only on status === 'trusted', and check that matchedName is the person you expect. See Recognise a user.

docs.title: 5. Decide where the template is kept
docs.text: By default the plugin keeps it in private app storage, out of device backups, and does not encrypt it. We recommend storing it encrypted: read it with getTrackerData() and put it back with loadTracker(). See Store the gallery.

docs.title: Get started with Flutter
docs.text:
Version 0.5.1, which uses the Android SDK 0.2.29 and the iOS SDK 0.11.0. Your app runs the camera and the capture loop, and the plugin gives you a result for each frame.

The plugin is installed from YEO's private Git repository, not from pub.dev. Ask YEO for access. The plugin README has every setup step in full, including the Android repository block and the iOS Podfile hook.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
dependencies:
  yeofr_flutter:
    git:
      url: https://github.com/YEOMessaging/yeofr-flutter
      ref: v0.5.1

Android:

  • Add YEO's Maven repository, using the address and login from YEO.
  • Add implementation 'com.yeomessaging:yeofr-android:0.2.29' to your app. The version must match exactly.
  • Build with compileSdk 36 and Android Gradle Plugin 8.9.1 or later.
  • Add the camera permission.

iOS:

  • Add NSCameraUsageDescription to Info.plist.
  • Add the download hook from the README to your Podfile, then run pod install. The minimum is iOS 17.0, on a real device only.

docs.title: 2. Start the plugin
docs.text:
await YeoFR.init(pilotUnlockCode: credentialFromYeo);
await YeoFR.createTracker();

final saved = await loadTrackerFromStorage();   // your own storage
if (saved != null) await YeoFR.loadTracker(saved);

On Android a refused credential throws a PlatformException with code INIT_ERROR. On iOS it closes the app. See Before you start.

docs.title: 3. Read results from the camera
docs.text:
Use the camera package. iOS needs bgra8888 and Android uses yuv420.

await controller.startImageStream((CameraImage image) async {
  final result = await YeoFR.detectFacesFromCameraImage(
    image: image,
    camera: camera,
  );
  // result.isLive, result.framing, result.faceIDs
});

docs.title: 4. Enrol the user
docs.text:
Each enroll call adds one sample, so one call gives you one sample. For a production enrolment, call it on several live, well-framed frames during a short guided capture, then save. See Enrol a user.

if (result.faceState == FaceState.detected && result.isLive) {
  final faceId = result.faceIDs.firstOrNull?.index;
  if (faceId != null) await YeoFR.enroll(faceId, 'user-id');   // 0 means success
}

// When the capture is finished:
final bytes = await YeoFR.saveTracker();
if (bytes != null) await saveTrackerToStorage(bytes);   // your own storage

docs.title: 5. Recognise the user
docs.text:
final recognised = result.isLive && result.faceIDs.firstOrNull?.id == expectedUser;

Accept once this has held for about a second. Never compare confidence with a number. See Recognise a user.

No depth check in Flutter

The plugin passes your camera frames to the SDK, so the iPhone's TrueDepth sensor is not part of the decision.

docs.title: Keep going
docs.text:
• Exclude your saved gallery from Android backup and device transfer. See Store the gallery.
  • Go-live checklist

docs.title: Get started on iOS
docs.text: Version 0.11.2. FaceTrustService is the quickest integration: it runs the camera, makes the trust decision and saves the enrolment.

docs.title: 1. Add the package
docs.text:
In Xcode choose File ▸ Add Package Dependencies… and enter the HTTPS address:

https://github.com/yeo-messaging/YEOFR-SPM

Choose exact version 0.11.2. Your deployment target must be iOS 17.0 or later.

Add the camera usage text to Info.plist, worded for your users:

<key>NSCameraUsageDescription</key>
<string>Used to verify your identity with face recognition.</string>

docs.title: 2. Start the service
docs.text:
import YEOFR

let service = FaceTrustService(pilotUnlockCode: credentialFromYeo)
// Attach service.previewSession to an AVCaptureVideoPreviewLayer.
try await service.start()

A refused credential closes the app

You cannot catch this. See Before you start.

docs.title: 3. Enrol the user
docs.text:
for await step in service.enroll(name: "user-id") {
    // step.phase: .capturing (show step.prompt), then .completed or .failed
}

One call captures one sample from the first frame that shows exactly one face. Call it again under other angles and lighting to add samples, up to 25.

This capture does not check liveness

Only start enrolment after you have confirmed who the user is by another means. Before you turn on face sign-in, require one .trusted result. See Enrol a user.

docs.title: 4. Recognise the user
docs.text:
for await update in service.updates() {
    // update.status: .noFace, .badFraming, .notTrusted or .trusted
    // update.matchedName, update.livenessGenuine, update.depthIsThreeD
}

Accept when update.status == .trusted and update.matchedName is the person you expect. With no enrolment in place, .trusted can be reported for any live face, so always check the name. See Recognise a user.

docs.title: 5. Decide where the enrolment is saved
docs.text: FaceTrustService saves the enrolment for you and restores it at the next launch. By default the file is unencrypted, sits in the app's Documents folder and is included in device backups. For production, move it and encrypt it. See Store the gallery.

docs.text:
• The simulator builds and runs your app, but every frame reports no face. Use a real iPhone.

docs.title: Get started with React Native
docs.text: Version 0.5.2, which uses the Android SDK 0.2.29 and the iOS SDK 0.11.0. The <YeofrCamera> view runs the camera and sends your JavaScript one result per analysed frame.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
npm i @yeomessagingcom/react-native-yeofr
npx yeofr-setup
npx yeofr-setup doctor

The setup command adds the iOS Swift package and the Android repository block, then runs pod install. doctor checks each step.

Then set these up by hand:

  • Android repository access. Put the address and login from YEO in ~/.gradle/gradle.properties, or in environment variables on your build server. Never commit them.
  • Android camera permission. The package declares no permissions. Add android.permission.CAMERA to your manifest and request it at runtime before you show the camera.
  • iOS deployment target. Set platform :ios to '17.0' in your Podfile, and add NSCameraUsageDescription to Info.plist.

Camera view on iOS

The iOS camera view needs React Native's old architecture, so set RCT_NEW_ARCH_ENABLED=0 if you use it. The other calls work with the New Architecture on, and so does the Android camera view.

The React Native guide covers manual setup, Xcode 26 and every option.

docs.title: 2. Activate
docs.text:
import {activate, loadTrackerFromDisk} from '@yeomessagingcom/react-native-yeofr';

await activate({pilotUnlockCode: credentialFromYeo});
const enrolled = await loadTrackerFromDisk();   // false if there is nothing to restore

On Android a refused credential rejects the call. On iOS it closes the app. See Before you start.

docs.title: 3. Enrol the user
docs.text:
Set enrolName on the camera and wait for the registered event. Then save.

<YeofrCamera
  style={StyleSheet.absoluteFill}
  enrolName={enrolling ? 'user-id' : undefined}
  enrolPoses={['front', 'yawLeft', 'yawRight', 'pitchUp', 'pitchDown']}
  onEvent={(e) => handle(e.nativeEvent)}
/>

if (event.type === 'registered') await saveTrackerToDisk();

On Android, enrolPoses makes the capture a paced walk that takes at least five seconds. On iOS the capture is a single front capture, whatever the poses list says. See Enrol a user.

docs.title: 4. Recognise the user
docs.text:
function handle(event: CameraEvent) {
  if (event.type !== 'result') return;
  const accepted = event.status === 'trusted' && event.matchedName === expectedUser;
}

Accept once this has held for about a second. Never compare confidence with a number. See Recognise a user.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
How to build each part of a face sign-in, and what we recommend.

If you want to Read Understand the pieces and how they fit How it works Capture a user's face well Enrol a user Decide when to accept a face Recognise a user Keep checking who is present during a session Verify throughout a session Understand the liveness check and its timing Liveness Write the on-screen messages and support replies Coach your users Decide where the enrolment is kept and how it is protected Store the gallery Move an existing app to the current version Upgrade and re-enrol Prepare a release Go-live checklist Fix a problem Troubleshooting

docs.title: Coach your users
docs.text: The SDK reports what it sees, and your app owns the wording. These messages are a good starting point. Most failed attempts come from lighting and position, and a clear message fixes many of them.

docs.title: On-screen messages
docs.text:
What the SDK reports What to show No face "Look at the camera" tooFar "Move closer" tooClose "Move back" multipleFaces "One face at a time" Badly placed, with no specific hint "Adjust your position" A face in view, liveness not confirmed yet "Checking…" Live, but not the enrolled person "Not recognised" trusted, or live with the expected name Your success state

Do not say 'spoof detected'

Real users see a "not live" reading during the warm-up. Show "Checking…" for the first few seconds, and show a failure only after the attempt time runs out.

docs.title: Give the user time
docs.text:
• Allow 5 to 10 seconds per attempt.
  • During the attempt, show the framing hint and "Checking…".
  • If time runs out, show the tips below and offer a retry.
  • After a few failed attempts, offer your fallback sign-in.

docs.title: If the right person is not recognised
docs.text:
Tell the user:

  1. Face a light, not a window. Remove sunglasses, a hat or a mask.
  2. Hold the phone at eye level, about 30 to 40 cm away, and follow the on-screen hint.
  3. Keep still and look at the screen for a second or two.
  4. Make sure no one else is in view.
  5. If it keeps failing in your usual place, set up face sign-in again there.

docs.title: What affects recognition
docs.text: Factor Effect Advice Light different from enrolment The most common cause of a missed match Face the light, and enrol in more than one light Head angle Looking well away from the camera lowers the match Look at the screen, and enrol with small head turns Distance Small faces carry less detail, and cut-off faces cannot be compared Follow the framing hint Glasses, hats, masks Can lower the match a lot See Enrol a user Ageing, a new beard, new glasses Gradual change may be absorbed, but a sudden large change may not Re-enrol after a large change Dirty lens Lowers the match Clean the lens

docs.title: A support reply you can reuse
docs.text:
After the update, face sign-in needs to be set up once more. Open the app, choose Set up face sign-in, face a light, and follow the prompts.

Use this wording when you move users to a new version.

docs.title: Verify throughout a session
docs.text: A login proves who opened a session. It does not prove who is still there. Because the SDK reports on every analysed camera frame, your app can keep checking that the right person is present, without asking the user to do anything.

docs.title: One-time and continuous checks
docs.text:
One-time check Continuous check When it checks Once, at login or at one action Throughout the period you choose What it shows The right person opened the session The right person is still present If the phone changes hands Not noticed Your app can react What the user does Takes a deliberate action Nothing, in normal use

It adds to your existing login and identity checks. It does not replace them.

docs.title: Choose when it runs
docs.text:
You set the policy. Common choices:

  • The whole session, from sign-in to sign-out.
  • Sensitive screens, such as account details or documents.
  • Critical moments, such as a high-value payment or a change to account settings.

Our advice: start with critical moments, then widen the policy once you have seen how it behaves with your users. The camera must be running throughout, so a narrower policy is easier on the battery and easier to explain.

docs.title: Decide what happens when the person is gone
docs.text:
The SDK gives your app the signal. Your app decides the response, for example:

  • ask the user to verify again;
  • hide sensitive content until the right person returns;
  • block high-risk actions;
  • flag the session for review;
  • end the session.

Use a stronger response for riskier actions. A person glancing away should not lose their session.

docs.title: How to read the signal
docs.text:
Use the same rule as at sign-in: live, and the expected person. See Recognise a user for the rule on each platform.

What your app sees What it probably means Live, with the expected name The right person is present No face The person looked away or left Not live, or framing is off The person moved, or the check is restarting Live, with another name or no name Someone else may be there More than one face Someone else has come into view

docs.title: Allow a grace period
docs.text:
Real users look away, move and pass through poor light, so do not react to one frame. When a face leaves, the match drops within a fraction of a second and the liveness answer expires within about 1.5 seconds. A face that returns needs about a second to be confirmed again.

Start with a grace period of a few seconds, and tune it by testing with your own users:

let lastConfirmed = Date.now();

function onResult(r) {
  if (r.status === 'trusted' && r.matchedName === expectedUser) {
    lastConfirmed = Date.now();
  } else if (Date.now() - lastConfirmed > GRACE_PERIOD_MS) {
    onPersonNotPresent();   // your policy
  }
}

This example uses the React Native, Capacitor and Cordova result fields. On other platforms, use the rule for your platform.

docs.title: What to plan for
docs.text:
• The app must be open. Expect no results while your app is in the background, and treat the return to the foreground as a new check.
  • Tell your users. Explain that the camera stays on during the session and why. Cover it in your privacy notice.
  • Battery and heat. Camera use and face processing draw power. Test sessions as long as your real ones, on the oldest phones you support.
  • Lighting changes. A long session can cross poor light, so make sure your response to a failed check is not harsh. See Coach your users.
  • No built-in history. These SDK versions do not keep a record of presence over time. If you need an audit trail, have your app record the events you care about.
  • Results stay local. The SDK does not sign its results. See Device and app security.
  • Capacitor and Cordova. The native camera preview sits behind your page, there is one camera session per app, and the screen stays in portrait. Plan your screens around this.

docs.title: Enrol a user
docs.text: A good enrolment is the best thing you can do for recognition later. This guide covers what to capture, how to protect the step, and how to do it on each platform.

docs.title: What we recommend
docs.text:
• Use a guided capture. Capture several samples with small head turns, and if possible in more than one light. One frame is enough to get started, but it can fail later when the light changes.
  • Confirm who the user is first. Run enrolment only after the user has signed in by another means.
  • Confirm the result. After the capture, require one successful recognition before you turn on face sign-in.
  • Use an opaque ID as the name. The name you pass is saved in the gallery, so use an internal customer ID rather than a real name.
  • Keep to one person per app installation. If you need several people, talk to YEO first.
  • Save straight away. Save the gallery as soon as the capture finishes, and offer a retry if saving fails.

docs.title: How many samples
docs.text:
Capture style Samples Typical time Quick capture One good frame About a second Guided capture (recommended for production) Up to 25, from several head angles About 5 seconds to around a minute, depending on your prompts

More varied samples make recognition more reliable, especially when the light changes.

docs.title: Protect the enrolment step
docs.text:
Enrolment decides whose face is trusted later, so it deserves the same care as setting a password.

On iPhone, the camera capture does not check liveness

On iOS, FaceTrustService.enroll(name:) stores the first frame that shows exactly one face. This also applies to the React Native, Capacitor and Cordova camera captures on iOS, because they use it. A photo held up to the camera could be stored.

To protect this step:

  1. Run enrolment only inside a session you already trust, after your own sign-in check.
  2. After the capture, require a trusted result with the expected name before you turn on face sign-in. trusted includes liveness.
  3. If that check does not pass, clear the enrolment and start again.

On Android, the React Native, Capacitor and Cordova captures only count live frames. In native Android and in Flutter your app calls enroll, so check liveness first, as the samples below do.

docs.title: How to enrol on each platform
What to tell the user
docs.text:
Before starting

  • Hold the phone upright, at eye level, and use the front camera.
  • Face a window or a lamp. Do not sit with a bright light behind your head.
  • Remove sunglasses, hats, hoods and face masks. Clear glasses you normally wear can stay on.
  • Make sure only your face is in view.

During the capture

  • Hold the phone about 30 to 40 cm away, with your whole face in the picture.
  • Look at the screen and hold still for a moment.
  • If prompted, turn your head slowly and only a little.
  • Keep the screen open until it says you are finished.

docs.title: Glasses and other changes
docs.text:
• Everyday glasses: enrol as the user normally appears. If they sometimes wear glasses and sometimes do not, capture part of the enrolment each way.
  • Sunglasses, hats, caps, hoods: remove them for enrolment, and ideally for sign-in.
  • Face masks over the nose and mouth: remove them for enrolment and sign-in. Face recognition is not designed to work with the lower face covered.

docs.title: Why an enrolment fails or comes out weak
docs.text:
Cause What the user notices Fix Strong light behind the user The capture does not progress, or recognition is unreliable later Turn round to face the light Very dim room The capture is slow or stalls Add light Face too far or too close "Move closer" or "Move back" Follow the hint Two faces in view "One face at a time" Make sure only the user is visible Moving a lot, or leaving the frame The capture stalls or restarts Hold still in front of the camera Single quick capture in one light Enrolment works, but recognition fails later in other light Use a guided capture, or re-enrol in typical conditions Screen closed early Fewer samples than intended Keep the screen open until the capture finishes

After about a minute without progress, show tips: face the light, adjust the distance, one face only.

docs.title: Go-live readiness checklist
docs.text:
Get your face sign-in integration ready for production.

This checklist helps you confirm that your YEO CFR SDK integration is configured correctly, thoroughly tested and ready for your users. Use it whether you are integrating for the first time or preparing an existing integration for release, and work through the sections that apply to you before you go live.

docs.title: 1. Access and credentials
docs.text:
Make sure your SDK credentials are configured securely and ready for production.

  • Load your YEO credential from your app configuration or backend, not from source code, so that a renewal does not need a new app release.
  • Confirm that the credential stays valid beyond your planned release date, and that someone is responsible for renewing it.
  • Test your release build with the credential you will ship, on both iOS and Android. A refused credential stops the SDK, and on iOS it closes the app.
  • Store your Android repository address and login securely. Do not commit them to source control.

docs.title: 2. User enrolment
docs.text:
A reliable face sign-in starts with a properly completed enrolment.

  • Users sign in through an existing method before they enrol their face. Here is why this matters.
  • Use a guided capture with multiple samples rather than a single frame.
  • Turn on face sign-in only after enrolment and a successful recognition check.
  • Enrol each face under an opaque identifier rather than the user's real name or other personal information.
  • Save the gallery as soon as the capture finishes, and handle a failed save.

docs.title: 3. Face recognition
docs.text:
Make sure your app handles recognition results correctly and consistently.

  • Accept a result only when the face is confirmed as live and matches the expected person. See Recognise a user.
  • Require the result to hold for about a second, rather than relying on a single frame.
  • Use the SDK's own decision: status or isLive, or faceState == Detected && isConfident() in native Android. Never compare confidence with a number.
  • Always provide another way to sign in if face recognition cannot be completed.
  • If you verify during a session, decide when it runs and what your app does when the person is no longer present. See Verify throughout a session.
  • For sensitive or high-value actions, add further authentication suited to your security requirements.

docs.title: 4. User experience
docs.text:
Clear guidance helps users complete face sign-in successfully.

  • Show a status such as "Checking…" during the first seconds. Do not show a failure while the SDK is still confirming liveness.
  • Make sure framing hints reach the user. See Coach your users.
  • Allow 5 to 10 seconds for each attempt, then show helpful tips and an option to retry.
  • Write a clear camera permission message that explains why your app needs the camera.
  • Handle a refused camera permission gracefully, including offering another way to sign in.
  • Lock the face recognition screen to portrait. Capacitor and Cordova require this.

docs.title: 5. Data protection and privacy
docs.text:
Face data needs protection throughout its lifecycle. Consider these recommendations alongside your organisation's data protection and privacy requirements. See Store the gallery for how to do each one.

  • Encrypt the gallery with keys held in the iOS Keychain or Android Keystore.
  • Exclude the gallery from cloud backups and device-to-device transfers.
  • When a user turns off face sign-in, delete the gallery, including any copies your app manages.
  • Make sure your privacy notice explains how biometric data is processed and stored on the device.
  • On Android, make sure your privacy notice and your Google Play Data safety form cover Google ML Kit's usage metrics. See What leaves the device.

docs.title: 6. Application and device security
docs.text:
The SDK provides face recognition and liveness. The overall security of your sign-in also depends on how your app and backend handle the results. Consider these points as part of your security assessment. See Device and app security.

  • Decide how your app handles rooted, jailbroken or otherwise tampered devices. The SDK does not check device integrity.
  • Decide whether to restrict screen capture and recording on the face recognition screen. The SDK does not do this.
  • Make sure your backend does not rely on a result from the app as its only proof of authentication. The SDK does not sign its results.
  • Apply suitable authentication, authorisation and further verification to sensitive operations.

docs.title: 7. Device compatibility and testing
docs.text:
Before you release to users, check your integration under realistic conditions.

  • Test on real iPhones and Android phones, not only on simulators or emulators.
  • Test in different lighting, including backlight and dim rooms.
  • Test with users wearing glasses, and with more than one face in view.
  • Test leaving the face recognition screen, sending the app to the background and coming back.
  • If your app uses a shielding or hardening product, run acceptance tests on a shielded build of the same commit. Develop and measure recognition on unshielded builds first, and expect screenshots of the face recognition screen to come out black when shielding is on.

  • Android: check that your release build meets Google Play's 16 KB memory page size requirement, using APK Analyzer or this command:

    zipalign -c -P 16 -v 4 app-release.apk

  • Android: test the first use on a real phone with Google Play services and a network connection, because the face detection model downloads at that point.

docs.title: 8. Support and upgrades
docs.text:
Prepare your own team for launch day.

  • Your support team has the coaching tips.
  • If this is an upgrade from an older SDK version, you have a re-enrolment plan.

docs.title: Ready for production?
docs.text:
Once you have completed the checks that apply to you, your integration is ready for your own production release assessment.

YEO provides the SDK and its face recognition and liveness capabilities. Your app remains responsible for the surrounding sign-in flow, credential management, data storage, privacy notices, backend validation and overall application security.

Need help? If you have questions about integration, configuration or production readiness before you go live, contact the YEO team.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The YEO CFR SDK (Continuous Facial Recognition) confirms that the right person is present, at sign-in and, if you choose, throughout the session. It has four parts, and all four run on the phone.

  1. Enrolment. The user looks at the camera once. The SDK turns the face into numeric samples.
  2. Saving. Your app saves the samples, called the gallery, and restores them at each launch.
  3. Recognition. While the camera runs, the SDK compares the face in view with the gallery.
  4. Liveness. At the same time, the SDK checks that a real person is in front of the camera, not a photo or a screen. On iPhones with a TrueDepth camera, the iOS camera path also checks depth.

Your app accepts the user only when recognition and liveness agree.

docs.title: Words used in these docs
docs.text: Term What it means Enrolment Capturing a user's face once so that it can be recognised later. Sample A compact numeric description of a face, computed on the phone from one camera frame. It is not a photo. Gallery The set of enrolled people and their samples. It is what your app saves and restores. The SDK's calls name it the tracker, as in saveTracker or loadTracker. Recognition Comparing the face in view with the gallery, and naming the person when the similarity is high enough. Liveness Judging whether the camera sees a real, present person rather than a photo, a screen or a mask. Framing hint Advice on where the face is: too far, too close, more than one face, or no face. It helps you guide the user.

docs.title: Who does what
docs.text: The SDK Your app Camera Runs it on iOS FaceTrustService, React Native, Capacitor and Cordova Runs it on native Android, Flutter and any custom frame input Decision Reports recognition and liveness for each frame Decides what to accept, and how long it must hold Screens Reports progress and hints Owns all wording, prompts and layout Gallery Produces it and reads it back Decides where it is kept and encrypts it Identity Compares faces Decides who the user is before enrolment Device trust Does not check it Checks for rooted or tampered devices if you need that

docs.title: How recognition decides
docs.text:
Each face becomes a sample, and the SDK compares it with every sample stored for each enrolled person. The best similarity counts, and higher means more alike. A match needs a similarity of at least 0.35, the default set by YEO from internal testing.

You do not need to pick a threshold. Use the result the SDK gives you. See Recognise a user.

docs.title: Getting better over time
docs.text:
Each person can hold up to 25 enrolment samples and up to 25 recent samples. Enrolment samples never change. Recent samples can be refreshed by successful recognitions, at most one per second, and the oldest is replaced first. Recognition can then follow gradual changes in lighting or appearance while staying anchored to the enrolment.

Platform How recent samples behave Android, on every plugin Learned while recognising. Kept only if your app saves the gallery after the session. iOS camera (FaceTrustService, React Native, Capacitor, Cordova) Learned while the app runs. The built-in service saves its file only at enrolment and deletion, so they are lost at the next launch unless your app saves the gallery itself. Flutter on iOS, and any custom frame input on iOS Not learned.

Our advice: plan for a good enrolment, and treat learning as a bonus.

docs.title: Different on Android and iPhone
docs.text:
Android iPhone Face detection Google ML Kit, through Google Play services Apple Vision, part of iOS Depth sensor Not used Part of the decision on the iOS camera path, when the phone has TrueDepth. Not used in Flutter. Too close or too far A hint only in native code. Bridges report badFraming. The built-in camera path reports badFraming and does not judge the face until it is well placed.

These differences are why we recommend testing on both platforms, with your own screens.

docs.title: Liveness
docs.text: The liveness check judges whether the camera sees a real, present person rather than a photo, a screen or a mask. It is passive: the user is never asked to blink, smile or turn. They just look at the camera.

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text:
• It needs a moment to start. When a face appears, the first answer usually takes about a second, and occasionally a few seconds. Show "Checking…", not an error.
  • It judges a sequence of frames. The check is continuous and does not rely on one snapshot. A brief dip does not flip the answer, because a confirmed answer is held for about a second.
  • It ends when the face goes. The answer expires within about 1.5 seconds. A face that returns starts the check again.
  • It judges one face. While a second face is in view, the frame is not accepted as live. The check resumes on its own when one face remains.

docs.title: What can make a real person read as not live
docs.text: Situation What happens What to tell the user The first moment after the face appears Not live during the warm-up Nothing. Show "Checking…". Strong light behind the head The answer can flicker Turn to face the light Very dim light Slower or unreliable answers Add light Too close, too far, or cut off Less reliable, or not judged until the face is well placed Follow the framing hint Two faces in view Not live until one face remains One face at a time Moving in and out of the frame Each return restarts the warm-up Stay in front of the camera Fast movement, blur, or glare on glasses Occasional short dips Hold still for a moment

docs.title: How your app should use it
docs.text:
1. Use the SDK's answer. Read isLive, or status where the plugin provides it. In native Android, use faceState == Detected && isConfident().
  2. Never compare confidence with a number. It is for display and debugging only, and its scale can change between SDK versions. Older versions used a bar of 0.71, which no longer applies.
  3. Combine it with recognition. See Recognise a user.
  4. Use the framing hint to guide, not to decide. It says "move closer", not "fail".

docs.title: Use the live camera
docs.text:
The check is designed for a live camera stream.

  • Frames your app supplies cannot prove the person is present. A recording fed in through your own pipeline defeats any liveness check.
  • Still-image matching (matchImage, enrollImage, imageMatchScore) runs no liveness at all.

docs.title: What it does and does not promise
docs.text:
The check is designed to refuse common presentation attacks, such as printed photos and photos or videos shown on phone, tablet and laptop screens. Like every liveness system, it lowers the risk and does not remove it.

It looks at what is in front of the camera. It does not check where the frames come from, so it cannot tell a real camera from a virtual one. See Device and app security.

For high-value actions, use it together with your app's other security measures.

docs.title: Recognise a user
docs.text: There is no "recognise" button to press. The SDK reports on every analysed frame, and your app decides when it has seen enough.

docs.title: The rule we recommend
docs.text:
Accept the user only when all of these are true:

  1. The SDK says the face is live.
  2. The SDK names the person you expect.
  3. Both have held together for about a second.

Do not accept on a single frame, and do not build your own rule from the numbers.

Always check the name

Check that the recognised name is the person you expect, even when the status already says trusted. On native iOS, with no enrolment in place, .trusted can be reported for any live face. Before you start recognition, also confirm that someone is enrolled.

docs.title: The rule on each platform
What the statuses mean
docs.text:
iOS, React Native, Capacitor and Cordova report one of four statuses.

Status Meaning What to show noFace No face in view "Look at the camera" badFraming A face is in view but cannot be used: too far, too close or badly placed The framing hint, or "Adjust your position" notTrusted A face that has not passed liveness or is not the enrolled person. With more than one face in view, some platforms report this instead of badFraming. See below trusted Live, and recognised Your success state

notTrusted covers several situations. You can tell them apart with isLive and matchedName, and with the framing hint for a second face:

Situation How to tell What to show More than one face detectedCount is above 1 "One face at a time" Liveness not confirmed isLive is false, whether or not matchedName is set "Checking…" Someone else isLive is true, matchedName is empty, and someone is enrolled "Not recognised" Nobody enrolled yet isLive is true, matchedName is empty, and nobody is enrolled Offer enrolment

docs.title: Timing
docs.text: Within about a second of looking at the camera, a real enrolled user is normally recognised and confirmed as live. In backlight or dim light it can take longer. Allow 5 to 10 seconds per attempt. See Coach your users.

docs.title: The limits of face recognition
docs.text:
• Very similar faces. Face recognition can confuse identical twins and sometimes close relatives. No face recognition system rules this out.
  • High-value actions. Use face sign-in as one factor, together with your other security checks.
  • One device, one person. Keep each installation to the person who enrolled on it.
  • Error rates. They depend heavily on your users, devices and lighting, so we do not quote a single figure. YEO can discuss an evaluation on your target devices.

docs.title: Recognition without the camera
docs.text: You can compare a still image with the gallery using calls such as matchImage in React Native or imageMatchScore on iOS. These run recognition only, with no liveness check, so they do not prove that the person is present.

docs.title: Store the gallery
docs.text: The gallery holds your user's face samples. Treat it as biometric data. The SDK produces it, and protecting it is your app's job: the SDK does not encrypt it for you in any default setup.

docs.title: What we recommend
docs.text:
1. Keep it on the device. Keep it in the app's private storage and do not sync it.
  2. Encrypt it yourself. Use a key held in the iOS Keychain or the Android Keystore.
  3. Exclude it from cloud backup and device-to-device transfer.
  4. Delete it when the user turns off face sign-in. Delete your own copies as well as the SDK's.
  5. Use an opaque ID as the enrolled name, so the file holds no real name.

docs.title: What is in it
docs.text:
• The names you enrolled, and when.
  • Numeric face samples: up to 25 from enrolment and up to 25 recent ones, per person.
  • The format version and the recognition model's version.

There are no photos or video.

Gallery Approximate size One sample 4 KB One person with all 25 enrolment samples 90 KB One person with both sets full 185 KB

docs.text: Platform Where it goes by default Encrypted In device backups Android Nowhere. The SDK gives your app the bytes. Your choice Your choice iOS with FaceTrustService A file in the app's Documents folder, saved after enrolment. You can pass another location as trackerURL. No Yes, unless you exclude it React Native A private file when you call saveTrackerToDisk(): Android files folder, iOS Application Support No Unless you exclude it, it follows your app's backup rules Flutter Nowhere. saveTracker() gives your app the bytes. docs.title: How to encrypt it
How to keep it out of backups
docs.text:
Android. Set android:allowBackup="false" and add android:dataExtractionRules that exclude the file. These cover cloud backup and device transfer.

iOS. Store the file outside Documents, for example in Application Support, and set isExcludedFromBackup on it. Turn on the Data Protection capability for the strongest protection your app can tolerate.

docs.title: How to delete it
docs.text:
Platform How to remove the enrolment Android YEOFRSDK.clearTracker(), then delete your stored copy. shutdown() alone does not clear enrolments from memory. iOS with FaceTrustService clearEnrollment() clears memory and removes the service's file. Delete any copy you hold yourself. React Native clearTracker(), then saveTrackerToDisk() to replace the saved copy. Confirm in your app that the next launch finds nobody enrolled. Flutter YeoFR.clearTracker(), then delete your stored copy Capacitor, Cordova clearTracker() removes the stored face. Delete any copy you hold yourself.

Uninstalling the app removes files in its private storage. Copies on your server or in a backup are yours to remove.

docs.title: Can we keep galleries on our server?
docs.text: You can. The gallery is available as bytes or as text, so it can be sent and stored as an opaque blob. It is still biometric data, so protect it in transit and at rest, and record which SDK version made it, because a gallery from an older recognition model cannot be loaded by a newer one.

docs.title: New phones
docs.text: Ask the user to enrol again on the new phone. It takes about a minute and gives the best results with that phone's camera.

docs.text: Contact YEO support. Tell us the SDK version, the platform and phone model, what you expected and what happened, and any error code. See what to include.

docs.title: Upgrade and re-enrol
docs.text: If your app is on an older version of the SDK, moving to the current one needs a one-time re-enrolment. This guide shows how to plan it so that your users hardly notice.

docs.title: Do users need to enrol again?
docs.text:
Moving from To Re-enrol? Android before 0.2.28 Android 0.2.29 Yes, once iOS before 0.11.0 iOS 0.11.0 or 0.11.2 Yes, once React Native 0.4.x or earlier React Native 0.5.2 Yes, once Flutter 0.2.x or earlier Flutter 0.5.1 Yes, once Android 0.2.28 Android 0.2.29 No iOS 0.11.0 iOS 0.11.2 No React Native 0.5.0 or 0.5.1 React Native 0.5.2 No Flutter 0.5.0 Flutter 0.5.1 No

The current versions use a new on-device recognition model, and the SDK refuses a gallery made by an older model. This is safe: nothing crashes, and the app simply has no enrolment until the user enrols again.

docs.title: What changes for your developers
docs.text:
• Liveness rule. Use isLive or status, or faceState == Detected && isConfident() in native Android. Remove any comparison with 0.71. In native Android, recompile every module that reads ANTI_SPOOF_THRESHOLD.
  • Android repository. The Android SDK moved to a new private repository with a new login from YEO. Update your maven { } block.
  • Android build. Your app needs compileSdk 36 and Android Gradle Plugin 8.9.1 or later. Google Play services is needed on the device.
  • iOS. iOS 17.0 or later is required. A few iOS calls became async, and the model-selection options are gone.
  • React Native on iOS. Camera enrolment is now a single front capture, so adjust any screen that prompted a walk on iOS.
  • Credential. A valid credential from YEO is required on both platforms.

docs.title: How to plan the re-enrolment
docs.text:
1. Before release, decide what the app will say, for example: "We've upgraded face sign-in. Please set it up again. It takes about a minute." Decide which fallback sign-in users have until they do.

  2. Detect the refused gallery at start-up, right after starting the SDK:

    Platform The sign Android loadTracker(...) returns a negative code. iOS with FaceTrustService enrolledName has no value after start(). React Native loadTrackerFromDisk() resolves false. Flutter loadTracker returns a negative code.

  3. Clean up. Delete the old stored gallery so that old biometric data does not linger. A refused file stays on disk until your app saves over it or deletes it. Delete galleries from older versions held on a server once the user has re-enrolled.

  4. Prompt the user to enrol with the guided capture, in their usual place and light.
  5. Save the new gallery straight away, and again after sign-in sessions.
  6. Roll out in stages if you can, and watch support contacts for "not recognised" in the first week. The usual causes are backlight and quick single-frame enrolments.

docs.title: What to tell your users
docs.text: After the update, face sign-in needs to be set up once more. Open the app, choose Set up face sign-in, face a light, and follow the prompts.

docs.title: Staying on the same version line
docs.text: Galleries carry over within the current versions. Check each release's notes for anything else you need to change. See Published versions.
